privacySections.title: 1. Overview
privacySections.body: PUZZLTHINK (the 'Service') can be played without an account. We only handle the information below when you choose to sign in with Google, send a bug report, or email us. Otherwise we do not receive personal information such as your name, email or phone number.

privacySections.title: 2. When you sign in with Google
privacySections.body:
• Account: your Google email address, name, profile photo and the unique ID Google issues — used to sign you in and run the Records page.
• Profile: the nickname you set on the Records page, whether you appear in the Hall of Fame, when you joined and when you were last seen.
• Game results: the game, mode (AI, friends or solo), win/loss or placing, per-game details such as difficulty, score or time, and when you played — used for your records and Hall of Fame ranking.
• Play time: total and per-day time, counted in one-minute steps while a game tab is visible.
If a game ends while you are signed out, its result is kept briefly in the browser's session storage so that signing in on the result screen can save that one game. It is cleared when you close the tab or press Quit or Play again.

privacySections.title: 3. When you send a bug report
privacySections.body: A report sent with the in-game 'Report a bug' button includes the category, what you wrote, a reply email (only if you enter one), the game and page address, your browser details (User-Agent), screen size, language, and your account ID if you are signed in. It is used only to look into the problem and reply.

privacySections.title: 4. When you email us
privacySections.body: Mail sent to contact@puzzlthink.com is forwarded to the operator's inbox with your email address and message. It is used only to reply and to review partnership proposals.

privacySections.title: 5. Statistics that cannot identify you
privacySections.body: For everyone, we count visitors per day and plays per game and mode as plain numbers. These counts contain no name, email, IP address or anything else that identifies you. To avoid counting the same visit twice in a day, the date of your visit is stored in your browser. To show how many people are online right now, a randomly generated device identifier and the time of your last visit are recorded in our database (Supabase) about every 45 seconds while a page is open. It cannot identify you and is deleted automatically 10 minutes after you leave.

privacySections.title: 6. Playing with friends (real-time)
privacySections.body: When you play with friends, the room code, the nickname you choose, a randomly generated device ID and your moves are relayed to the other players in the room through a real-time service (Supabase Realtime). This is used only for live relay and is not stored in our database. The host's browser may keep the game state so the match can continue.

privacySections.title: 7. Information stored in your browser
privacySections.body: Local game records, tutorial status, nickname, last game settings, sign-in state and visit date are stored in your browser's local storage. You can delete them at any time by clearing site data in your browser settings; this resets local records and settings and signs you out.

privacySections.title: 8. Retention and deletion
privacySections.body:
• Account information, profile, game results and play time: kept until you ask us to delete them, then deleted without delay.
• Bug reports: kept as long as needed to investigate and reply, and deleted without delay on request.
• Emails: kept as long as needed to reply or review a proposal, and deleted without delay on request.
Electronic records are deleted so that they cannot be restored.

privacySections.title: 9. What is public, and sharing with third parties
privacySections.body: If you are signed in, have the Hall of Fame option on and make the top ranks, your nickname, profile photo, wins and games played are visible to anyone on the Records page. Your email is never shown, and turning the option off on the Records page removes you immediately. Otherwise we do not sell or share personal information with third parties, except when legally required through due process.

privacySections.title: 10. Service providers and international transfer
privacySections.body:
We rely on the providers below, whose servers are outside Korea (Supabase in the Asia-Pacific region, the others mainly in the United States). Information is sent over the network when you use the Service, and each provider uses it only for the work we give them.
• Supabase (Asia-Pacific region servers): sign-in, database (profiles, game results, bug reports, statistics) and real-time play
• Vercel: website hosting and delivery (including access logs)
• Google: Google sign-in, Google AdSense ads, Google Analytics visit statistics and the operator's inbox (Gmail)
• Web3Forms: relays bug reports to the operator's email
• Forward Email: forwards mail sent to contact@puzzlthink.com to the operator's inbox
If you do not want your information transferred abroad, you can play without signing in or sending reports, or ask us to delete it. All games remain available either way.

privacySections.title: 11. Your rights
privacySections.body: You can ask at any time to see, correct, delete or stop the processing of your personal information. You can change your nickname and Hall of Fame visibility yourself on the Records page; for anything else, email contact@puzzlthink.com and we will act without delay once we confirm it is you. Legal guardians of children under 14 have the same rights.

We also use Google Analytics to collect visit statistics (pages viewed, time on page, referring site, device and browser type, approximate location). WallGoGuide.title: Wallgo Online — the Devil's Plan game, on the web
WallGoGuide.intro: Wallgo is a territory strategy game that became a fan favorite on Netflix's brain-survival show The Devil's Plan. If you enjoy shows like The Genius, it will feel right at home. PUZZLTHINK brings Wallgo to the web so anyone can play against two AI opponents right in the browser.
rules: On a 7×7 board, each player places 2 pieces in the order 1→2→3→3→2→1.

On your turn you have 90 seconds to move one piece 0–2 tiles up, down, left or right. Two tiles may be straight or turn a corner, and you may stay put. You cannot pass through other pieces or walls, and a piece that cannot step at all cannot stay and build either.
After moving, you must build a wall on one open side of that piece. If time runs out, a wall is placed on a random side.
In 3-player games, once per game each player may knock down one wall next to their piece. The piece can still move afterwards.

The game ends when every piece is sealed in its own space. The most tiles in the spaces containing your pieces wins, and a tie is a shared win. If several players are locked in together with no one able to move, each piece scores only the tile it stands on.

faq.q: Where can I play Wallgo?
faq.a: Right here on PUZZLTHINK — in any desktop or mobile browser, with no sign-up or install.

faq.q: Is it the same game as on The Devil's Plan?
faq.a: It is built on the core rules seen on the show — moving, building walls, and scoring territory — adapted for solo play against AI.

faq.q: Is it free?
faq.a: Yes, every game is free.

faq.q: Is there a 2-player (1:1) mode?
faq.a: Yes. You can play a 3-player game against two AI opponents, or a 1:1 duel with 4 pieces each, like round 2 on the show. AI difficulty can be Easy, Normal, or Hard.

A draw decides who goes first; the remaining 2 pieces are placed first→second→second→first.
Moving and wall building work as in the 3-player game, but there is no wall break.
The game ends when the two players are fully separated, and the larger territory wins.
WallGoGuide.strategyIntro: In Wallgo, opening placement and the position of a single wall can decide the game. Here are common situations drawn on the board. Columns are A–G and rows are 1–7 from the top.
legend: Side you could close but should leave

strategies.title: Anchor near a corner
strategies.body: Just as corners are easy to secure in Go, pieces near C3, E3, C5, or E5 can lock in territory with few walls. In a 3-player game, though, two opponents can close your two outer sides together and trap you in a few corner tiles, so keep an exit open.

strategies.title: The center D4 is stronger than it looks
strategies.body: Unlike a 19-line Go board, a 7×7 board brings fights to the center immediately. D4 can move two tiles in all four directions, giving the most mobility and a great spot to cut opponents’ expansion routes.

strategies.title: Never sit inside three walls
strategies.body: With walls on three sides, one more wall from an opponent leaves that piece unable to move. Unless you have a specific plan, never step into such a spot, and get out as soon as a third wall appears.

strategies.title: Two walls is risky in a 3-player game
strategies.body: With two opponents, a spot with two walls can be sealed in a single round, one wall each. Trapping one player helps the other two, so these team-ups happen naturally. If both opponents are nearby, avoid two-wall spots too.

strategies.title: Lock an opponent into a corner
strategies.body: Walls are not only for growing your own area. Trap an opponent in a few corner tiles and the rest of the board is split among everyone else, effectively removing them from the race for first. Move toward the spot that closes their last exit.

strategies.title: Do not close awkward territory for them
strategies.body: There is no need to seal an opponent’s narrow, hard-to-grow area. The game only ends when every space is split, so closing it just saves them turns. Left open, they must keep building walls inside the strip and shrink it themselves.

strategies.title: Block with your own pieces
strategies.body: No piece can move through another piece. In the 3-player game a wall can be broken once, but a path blocked by a piece cannot. Parking a piece in the middle of an opponent’s corridor is a more reliable block than a wall.

strategies.title: Wall break is all about timing
strategies.body: Breaking and moving are separate steps: first knock down one wall next to your piece, then move 0–2 squares as usual. You only get one. Save it to flip the game at the end, or use it mid-game to cross into open space first and build momentum. Too late and the board is already decided; too early and you have nothing left in a crisis. An opponent about to close their region is a strong signal.

JanggiGuide.title: 12 Janggi Online — the game from The Genius
JanggiGuide.intro: 12 Janggi is a mini chess that became famous in the final of the brain-survival show The Genius. Just 4 pieces on 12 squares, but captured pieces can be dropped back in, so every move counts. Play the AI or invite a friend with a link.
rules: Two players play on a 3-wide, 4-tall board of 12 squares. The row nearest each player is their camp.
Each starts with 將, 相, 王 and 子 on fixed squares: 將 on the camp’s right, 相 on its left, 王 in the middle and 子 in front of 王.
Players alternate moving one piece one step in a marked direction. Pieces cannot rotate.
Moving onto an enemy piece captures it; it joins your hand and can be used from your next turn whenever you like.
Dropping a captured piece also uses a turn. You cannot drop onto an occupied square or into the enemy camp.
A 子 that enters the enemy camp flips to 侯. A captured 侯 is used as 子.
Capture the enemy 王 to win. You also win if your 王 enters the enemy camp and survives until your next turn.

JanggiGuide.pieceDesc_wang: All 8 directions. Losing it ends the game.
JanggiGuide.pieceDesc_hu: Promoted 子. All but the back diagonals.

special.title: Dropping pieces
special.body: Dropping uses your turn. Gold dots show legal squares; the red X marks the enemy camp where drops are not allowed.

special.title: 子 promotes to 侯
special.body: A 子 reaching the enemy camp flips to the much stronger 侯. If you capture a 侯, it comes back as 子.

special.title: King entry win
special.body: If your 王 enters the enemy camp and they cannot capture it before your next turn, you win. Check every attacker before you step in.

JanggiGuide.strategyIntro: With so few pieces, one mistake decides the game. Here are common situations.

strategies.title: Count the opening pawn trade
strategies.body: The first player can take the enemy 子 at once, but the enemy 王 recaptures right away. Moving first means seizing the initiative; moving second means punishing overreach.

strategies.title: Bring the king forward
strategies.body: The king is your most mobile piece. One step forward it protects your other pieces and blocks the enemy king’s path. Just never step onto a square an enemy piece attacks.

strategies.title: 子 < 相 < 將
strategies.body: Generally a 相 is worth more than a 子 and a 將 more than a 相. When trading, compare what you give and get — and remember captured pieces come back as drops.

strategies.title: Pieces that guard each other
strategies.body: Two 相 linked on a diagonal recapture for each other. Shapes where pieces support one another make it hard for the opponent to break in.

strategies.title: Plan where drops can go
strategies.body: Drops cannot enter the enemy camp, so attacking drops need open middle squares. Rather than rushing, drop decisively onto the enemy king’s path or next to your own king.

strategies.title: Stop entry threats at once
strategies.body: If the enemy king reaches the square in front of your camp, guard its entry squares now. With so few possibilities, reading 3–5 moves ahead decides games.

SudokuGuide.title: Online Sudoku — rules and solving techniques
SudokuGuide.intro: Sudoku is a logic puzzle, not a math one. You fill the empty squares of a 9×9 grid following three simple rules, so it takes a minute to learn — but harder puzzles reward thinking several steps ahead. PUZZLTHINK Sudoku offers Easy, Medium and Hard, and every puzzle can be solved by logic alone, without guessing.
rules: The 9×9 grid has 9 rows, 9 columns and nine 3×3 boxes outlined in bold.
Each row contains the digits 1 to 9 exactly once.
Each column contains the digits 1 to 9 exactly once.
Each 3×3 box contains the digits 1 to 9 exactly once.
Given digits cannot be changed; fill every empty square to finish. On PUZZLTHINK the game ends after 3 mistakes.
SudokuGuide.techniquesIntro: The blue square is the one being solved; light blue lines are the rows, columns or box that prove it.

techniques.title: 1. Cross-hatching
techniques.body: To place a 5 in the top-left box, cross out the rows and columns that already contain a 5 in other boxes. With rows 2–3 and columns 1–2 blocked, only one square is left — that is the 5. This is the first technique to learn.

techniques.title: 2. One square left in a line
techniques.body: If a row already has eight digits, the missing digit goes in the last empty square. Start each puzzle by scanning rows, columns and boxes with only one or two blanks — every easy square adds clues elsewhere.

techniques.title: 3. Only one candidate
techniques.body: The center square’s row already has 1, 2 and 3, its column has 4, 5 and 6, and its box has 7 and 8. With 1–8 ruled out, the only possible digit is 9. This checks a row, column and box at once for a single square.

techniques.title: 4. Notes and pairs
techniques.body: If two squares in a row both have only 2 and 7 as candidates, those digits must go in those two squares. You can then remove 2 and 7 from every other square in that row. Turn on notes (space bar) to spot pairs like this.

levels.title: Easy
levels.body: Many givens; cross-hatching and scanning are enough. Great for learning the rules.

levels.title: Medium
levels.body: You will need to find single-candidate squares. A few notes keep you moving.

levels.title: Hard
levels.body: Few givens; notes and pair elimination are essential. Fill only the squares you are sure of.

faq.a: Once per game, a hint fills in the correct digit for the easiest empty square right now. Use it to get unstuck; to improve, try the techniques above first.

faq.a: Turn on notes with the button or the space bar to pencil in small candidate digits. Turn it off to return to normal input.

faq.a: Yes. Every puzzle has exactly one solution and can be solved by logic without guessing.

Heavy13Guide.title: Heavy 13 — The Devil's Plan prison match, on the web
Heavy13Guide.intro: Heavy 13 is the 7-player game from the first prison match of The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Players stack rocks on red, green and blue stands; whoever pushes a stand to 13 or more takes all the rocks that were there. It is less about arithmetic and more about reading where everyone else will play. Play six AIs right away, or invite friends and let AI fill the empty seats.
rules: Seven players each get rock cards 0–6, two chips each of red, green and blue, and one rainbow chip.
Each round, everyone secretly plays one rock card and one color chip at the same time. The chip picks the stand; the card is the rock's weight.
Once all have played, chips then cards are revealed and the placement order is set: rainbow first, then higher cards, ties clockwise from the start player.
Players place in order. A rainbow chip lets you choose the stand when you place.
On your turn you may pass once per round. Passers place after everyone else, and the first to pass places last.
If your rock brings a stand to 13 or more, the rocks already there are collected and you take one penalty per rock. Your rock stays on the stand.
The last player penalized in a round becomes the next start player.
After round 7 everyone gets a fresh set of cards and chips; the stands carry over. The game lasts 14 rounds.
Fewer penalties rank higher; on a tie, the more recent penalty ranks lower. 1st wins; 6th and 7th are eliminated.
Heavy13Guide.orderBody: Round 1 from the show: with ④ as start player (★), the two 6s go first (⑤ is closer clockwise from ④, so it is #1), then the five 5s go clockwise from ④.
Heavy13Guide.orderCaption: Chip color · rock card · resulting order (#)
Heavy13Guide.collapseBody: Red holds 6 and 5 (11). Adding a 5 makes 16: the two rocks already there are collected for 2 penalty points, and the new 5 stays alone on the stand.
Heavy13Guide.passBody: If A then B pass, C and D place first, then B, and A places last. The earlier you pass, the later you place — often after a stand has been cleared.

strategies.title: 0 is your best shield and weapon
strategies.body: A 0 never adds to the total, so you cannot collapse a stand with it, yet it adds a cube that raises the next collapser's penalty. Save it for when all three stands are dangerous.

strategies.title: One priority pass per hand
strategies.body: The rainbow chip lets you place first, once per hand. Use it to claim a stand before big rocks land, or to dodge a crowded color. Paired with a low card and a pass, it can also pick the safest stand at the very end.

strategies.title: Play high, then pass
strategies.body: A high card places early, but passing sends you to the back. The idea is to let someone collapse a stand first and then drop into the cleared stand. If you picked a dangerous stand alone, though, passing does not help.

strategies.title: The fresh hand is the turning point
strategies.body: Round 8 deals a new hand like round 1, but the stands are already loaded. You may need your rainbow or 0 immediately.

strategies.title: Leave a little room rather than filling to 12
strategies.body: A stand filled to 12 scares everyone away and just intensifies the fight elsewhere. Leaving 1–2 points of room tempts several players to think "a 1 alone is safe" — and they collapse it on each other. On the other hand, if you have used up that color and will not go there again, blocking it on purpose fuels everyone else's guessing game.

strategies.title: Count the remaining cards and chips
strategies.body: Every revealed card and chip is public. Track who has used up which colors and who still holds big rocks to predict which stand will be crowded next.

faq.q: Do I need 7 people?
faq.a: No. Solo play uses six AIs. In a friend room, choose 4–7 total players and turn AI filling off to wait until every selected seat is occupied by a friend.

faq.q: Can I see others' cards before the reveal?
faq.a: No. Chips and cards stay hidden until everyone has submitted.

faq.q: What if I run out of time?
faq.a: When the submission timer ends, a random card and chip are submitted for you; on your placement turn, you place automatically after 20 seconds.

faq.q: Is it free?
faq.a: Yes, every game is free.

Heavy13Guide.motifBody: It closely resembles the card game 6 nimmt!: you add numbers to a chosen row and whoever crosses the threshold takes the penalty. The differences: a start player, the rainbow chip and pass rule that reduce pure luck, and a threshold based on the total (13) rather than the number of cards.

nineMensMorris.tagline: Nine pieces each, 24 points. Line up three to take your opponent's pieces one by one.
nineMensMorris.players: 2 (1:1 with the AI or a friend)
nineMensMorris.pace: No limit vs AI · 30–90s turns with friends
rules: Black and white take turns placing nine pieces each on empty points. Nothing moves until all are placed.
Then each turn, move one piece along a line to a free neighbouring point.
Three of yours in a straight line (a mill) takes one enemy piece. Pieces in a mill are safe.
Down to three pieces you may fly anywhere; two pieces or no move loses. Best of three!
nineMensMorris.origin: Nine Men's Morris was the first game of the final in Netflix's The Devil's Plan season 1. It is a board game thousands of years old (also called Mill); as on the show, a deadlock with three pieces left ends after ten turns and the side with fewer pieces loses.

gyulhap.tagline: Read three attributes, find every Hap, then claim the final Gyul.
rules: Nine of 27 cards are shown each round; every card combines a shape, ink color and background.
Pick three whose values are all same or all different in every attribute: a correct Hap scores +1, a miss −1.
When no unclaimed Hap remains, call Gyul for +3; call too early and lose 1.
Solo play chases a high score before time expires; friend matches compare scores after ten rounds.
gyulhap.origin: A web adaptation of Gyul! Hap! from the final of The Genius: Rules of the Game, with solo timed challenges and a 2–4 player buzzer match.

indianPoker.tagline: See their card, never yours. Take every chip through betting and bluffing.
indianPoker.pace: Until one stack is empty · 20–45 s friend turns
rules: Start with 20 chips each and a 20-card deck containing two copies of 1–10.
You see only the opponent's forehead card, then bet, call, raise or fold.
At showdown the higher card wins the pot; equal cards carry the pot into the next hand.
Folding a 10 pays 10 extra chips. Empty your opponent's stack to win.
indianPoker.origin: Built from the Indian Poker rules used in the final of The Genius: Rules of the Game.

laserJanggi.tagline: Turn the mirrors, engineer the light path, and strike the enemy king first.
laserJanggi.pace: Friend games: 30, 60 or 90 seconds per turn
rules: On the 8×8 board, move one piece a single square in any of eight directions, or rotate it 90°. The laser cannot move.
Your laser fires automatically after the action. Mirrors reflect it; the splitter sends it straight and reflects a second beam.
Triangle and square knights are removed when struck on a non-mirrored side. Lasers and splitters are beam-proof.
A king is removed by a beam from any direction. Strike the enemy king first to win.
laserJanggi.origin: A web adaptation of Laser Janggi from the death match in The Genius: Rule Breaker, using the broadcast board's 8×8 setup and explicit beam tracing.

blindGomoku.tagline: Black and white hide behind color. Remember, deduce, and connect five first.
blindGomoku.pace: No limit vs AI · 30–90 s turns with friends
rules: You play first as black and the AI follows as white, but the sides stay hidden during play.
Choose one of seven surface colors; the AI answers with a stone of that same color.
There are no forbidden moves. The first side to connect five or more wins.
Twice per game, flip the board to inspect the hidden position for five seconds.
blindGomoku.origin: A gomoku variant inspired by blind gomoku on Netflix's The Devil's Plan. When the game ends the board flips to show black, white and the winning line, and you can replay on either side.

wallgo.tagline: Move your characters, build walls, and claim more territory than anyone else.
rules: Each player places pieces on a 7×7 board: 2 each in the 3-player game, 4 each in 1:1.
On your turn, move one piece 0–2 squares up, down, left or right (two squares may turn a corner, and staying put is allowed), then you must build a wall on one of its four sides.
In the 3-player game, each player may once per game knock down one wall next to their piece and then move it.
When every player's space is sealed off, the game ends and the largest total area containing your pieces wins. A tie is a shared win.
wallgo.origin: A territory game from the Netflix brain-survival show The Devil's Plan. Both the round 1 three-player game and the round 2 one-on-one game are included.

russianRoulette.tagline: Track the loaded chambers, turn the muzzle, and survive the final trigger sequence.
russianRoulette.pace: 60 s per turn in friend rooms · no limit vs AI
russianRoulette.friend: Link or 4-digit invite code, AI fills seats
rules: Two rounds are hidden among six chambers, and each player gets 16 secret credits.
Inspect two adjacent chambers publicly (1 credit) or privately (2 credits), or turn the muzzle 1 step (3 credits) or 2 steps (4 credits).
Secretly pay 1–3 manipulation credits into a shared pool; whoever brings it to 6 swaps the two adjacent chambers they chose.
When three players run out of credits, firing starts at the muzzle and goes clockwise; the two players hit are eliminated.
russianRoulette.origin: The Russian roulette prison match from Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again, played with the same rules as the show.

heavy13.tagline: Push a stand to 13 and take the penalty! A mind game for 4–7.
heavy13.pace: 14 rounds · friend rooms: 90 s to submit, 20 s to place
heavy13.friend: 4–7 players, friends only or AI fill
rules: Each player gets seven rock cards (0–6), two red, green and blue chips, and one rainbow chip.
Every round everyone secretly plays one card and one chip at once: the chip picks the stand, the card is the rock's weight.
The rainbow chip places first (and picks its stand), then higher numbers. Ties go clockwise from the start player, and once per round you may pass to place later.
Whoever pushes a stand to 13 or more takes a penalty for each rock already on it. After 14 rounds the fewest penalties wins.
heavy13.origin: The first prison match of The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). Taking a penalty for crossing a threshold closely resembles the card game 6 nimmt!.

janggi.tagline: Capture the king or march into the enemy camp. A sharp duel on 12 squares.
janggi.pace: Friend rooms: 90, 60 or 30 s per turn
rules: On a 3×4 board, each player starts with four pieces: General, Minister, King and Pawn.
Take turns moving one piece one square in a direction it shows. Captured pieces become yours and can be dropped back from your next turn.
A Pawn that enters the enemy camp flips into a stronger Lord.
Win by capturing the enemy King, or by moving your King into the enemy camp and surviving a turn there.
janggi.origin: A mini chess made famous by the brain-survival show The Genius (seasons 3 and 4).

russianJanggi.tagline: Tic-tac-toe where big pieces swallow small ones. 10 seconds per move.
russianJanggi.pace: 10 s per turn · no-limit option vs AI
rules: On a 3×3 board, each player has 2 large, 2 medium and 2 small pieces.
On your turn, place a new piece or move one of yours on the board. Large covers medium and small; medium covers small.
Own three in a row to win. If moving a piece reveals the opponent's row underneath, they win.
Out of time, or nowhere to play, and the turn passes.
russianJanggi.origin: The Russian Janggi game from The Society Game 2, playable on the web: a 3×3 strategy game that adds covering and moving pieces to tic-tac-toe.

sudoku.tagline: A timeless number puzzle that starts light and keeps you thinking.
sudoku.pace: No time limit · solve time recorded
sudoku.solo: 3 levels, one hint per game, notes
rules: Fill the 9×9 grid so every row, column and 3×3 box holds 1 to 9 exactly once.
Given numbers can't be changed; the puzzle is done when every cell is filled.
Three mistakes and the game is over.
Every puzzle has exactly one solution and can be solved by logic alone.
sudoku.origin: A classic puzzle solved with logic, not arithmetic. The rules take a minute to learn, but harder puzzles need reasoning several steps ahead.

nemoCount.tagline: Find every rectangle whose numbers add up to the target, without missing one.
nemoCount.pace: Challenge 30 min · friend games 1–5 min per problem or untimed
nemoCount.friend: 2–6 players, buzzer, retry after a miss, agreed passes, link or 4-digit code
rules: The board is made of square cells; some carry numbers. Blank cells count as 0.
A "nemo" is any rectangle of whole cells (squares and single cells included) that lies entirely inside the board.
Count how many rectangles have numbers adding up exactly to the target.
Solo, see how many you solve in 30 minutes; with friends, whoever buzzes first answers within 10 seconds.
nemoCount.origin: Based on Nemo Count from Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3); boards are generated at random and every answer and solution is computed automatically.

blackWhite.tagline: Tiles 0–8, but only their colour shows. Read your rival's numbers and take rounds with the bigger tile.
blackWhite.pace: 3–5 minutes a game · friend turns 15–60 s
rules: Both players get the same nine tiles, 0 to 8. Even tiles (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) are black; odd tiles (1, 3, 5, 7) are white.
The leader lays a tile face down and only its colour is shown; the other player answers after seeing that colour.
The higher number scores a point; equal numbers are a draw. Your rival's numbers stay hidden until the end.
The round winner leads next (after a draw the leader stays). The game ends after nine rounds or once it is decided.
blackWhite.origin: A web adaptation of Black & White from the death match in The Genius: Rule Breaker. You never see your rival's numbers while playing; at the end every tile is turned over and you can replay the mind game round by round.

blackWhite2.tagline: A blind auction across nine rounds with 99 points. Read colours and gauges instead of exact bids.
blackWhite2.pace: 5–10 minutes a game · friend turns 30–60 s
blackWhite2.ai: 1v1, three AI levels using public information only
rules: Both players receive 99 points for up to nine rounds. Spend any amount each round; spent points are gone.
The leader bids first. A bid from 0 to 9 shows as black and 10 or more as white; the exact number stays hidden.
The higher bid scores one and leads next. Equal bids score nothing and the existing leader stays.
Remaining points appear as one of five bands, from 0–19 to 80–99. The leader's gauge updates the instant they bid.
First to five, or the higher score after round nine, wins. A round-nine tie resets both players to 33 points for a best-of-three overtime.
blackWhite2.origin: A web adaptation of Black & White II from a death match in The Genius: Black Garnet. After the game, every hidden bid is revealed and the replay calls out close wins, bait, overspending and pressure.

piggyBank.tagline: Remember the black and white coins in each piggy bank, answer right, and doubt wrong answers to score.
piggyBank.friend: 2–4 players, AI fills seats · link or code
rules: Everyone gets a piggy bank holding 1 black and 1 white coin in their lower slot; the first player also gets bank 5 on top.
On your turn put 1–5 coins in your lower bank, say what you put in, and hand it to anyone. Your top bank drops to the lower slot.
The receiver says how many coins of the asked colour (black, white, black…) their top bank holds, within 20 seconds.
Others may doubt within 10 seconds: a wrong answer gives the doubter +1 and the answerer −1; a right one costs the doubter 1. First to 5 points ends the game.
piggyBank.origin: A web adaptation of the Piggy Bank prison match from Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again. Coin drops are shown only briefly and never logged — it's all memory.

hexagon.tagline: Memorize 19 numbers, then name the lines of three that add up to the target by their letters.
hexagon.pace: 1–2 min per round · 10 rounds or a 10-min challenge
hexagon.level: Memory + mental math (random boards · the 10 broadcast boards)
hexagon.friend: 2–4 players, buzz then declare within 10 s, +1 right / −1 wrong, link or 4-digit code
rules: 19 hexagons sit in rows of 3, 4, 5, 4 and 3. The front of each shows a number, the back a letter from A to S.
Each round the numbers are shown for 30 seconds, then the board flips to its letters and the target number appears.
Name a straight line of three neighbouring tiles (across or along a diagonal) whose numbers add up to the target. Right +1, wrong −1.
Repeating an answer already given is wrong too, and given answers are not marked, so remember them. A round ends when every answer is out or after 90 seconds without one.
hexagon.origin: Based on Hexagon, the second game of the final of Netflix's The Devil's Plan season 1. Boards and targets are generated at random and every answer is computed; the ten boards from the broadcast are included.

slitherlink.tagline: A logic puzzle: join the dots into one unbroken loop that runs along exactly as many sides as each number says.
slitherlink.solo: New challenge (ranked) · beat a board · practice
slitherlink.friend: 2–4 race on the same board · first loop wins · link or 4-digit code
slitherlink.ai: New challenge (ranked) · beat a board · practice
rules: Join neighbouring dots into a single closed loop with no branches or loose ends.
A number in a cell is how many of its four sides the loop runs along. 0 means none.
Cells without a number can have any number of sides used.
Mark sides you know are empty with ✕ so you do not lose track.
slitherlink.origin: The line puzzle played on the show, brought to the web: the same 11×11 board, with random boards that each have exactly one answer.

wallgo2.tagline: The game from The Devil's Plan 3 prison match, episode 10! Build walls with square and round pieces and claim the most ground.
rules: 7×7 board. Round 1 (3 players): one square and one round piece each. Round 2 (1:1): 2 square + 2 round, the round ones on fixed tiles.
Players place in turn order, then the second piece in reverse order.
On your turn, move one piece (square: 1–2 tiles straight; round: 1 tile, may turn for 1 more) and build a wall beside it. No staying put.
In round 1 only, each player may once break a wall on their path.
When every piece is separated, the most tiles wins; ties go to the bigger single area.
wallgo2.origin: The follow-up to Wallgo from The Devil's Plan 3 prison match, episode 10. Both round 1 (3 players) and round 2 (1:1) are here.

RussianRouletteGuide.title: Russian Roulette online — The Devil's Plan prison match on the web
RussianRouletteGuide.intro: Russian Roulette is a deduction game for six players around one revolver. Two of its six chambers are loaded, and each player spends 16 credits to inspect chambers, turn the muzzle or secretly swap chambers. When the shots are fired, the two players hit are out and four survive. It brings the Russian roulette prison match from Netflix's "The Devil's Plan: Dead Again" to the web with the same rules as the show, against AI or in a friend room. It is a brain game with nothing to do with real firearms.
rules: Six players sit in a circle. Two of the revolver's six chambers are loaded at random, and the muzzle starts pointing at a random player.
Everyone gets 16 private credits. Starting with the start player and going clockwise, each player takes one action at a time; the start player moves one seat each round.
Public inspection (1 credit): open two adjacent chambers and show the result to everyone.
Private inspection (2 credits): look at two adjacent chambers yourself. Others only see that you inspected.
Turn the muzzle 1 seat (3 credits) or 2 seats (4 credits) clockwise. Everyone sees the turn.

Manipulation (1–3 credits): everyone secretly pays into one shared pool. Whoever brings it to 6 swaps the contents of two adjacent chambers they choose, and the pool resets to 0; anything over 6 is lost. Who paid what is revealed after the shots.
A player with no credits left skips their turns. The moment three players have spent all their credits, the shots are fired.
Firing starts with the player the muzzle points at and goes clockwise, one chamber per player. The two players hit are out; the other four survive.
RussianRouletteGuide.specialTitle: Rules that are easy to miss

special.title: Who gets hit depends on the muzzle and the chambers
special.body: When firing, the first chamber goes to the player the muzzle points at, the second to the next player clockwise, and so on. If you know where both bullets are and where the muzzle points, you can work out the two players who will be hit.

special.title: Public and private intel are tracked separately
special.body: Public results appear for everyone under confirmed bullet positions; private results stay on your screen with a lock icon. Tap a character to mark who you think will be hit.

special.title: Manipulation happens silently
special.body: When chambers are swapped there is no notice, so intel you gathered earlier can quietly become wrong. Only the player who made the swap knows the new contents of those two chambers.

special.title: Running out of credits ends the game
special.body: As soon as three players have no credits left, the shots are fired, no matter how many credits the others still hold. Keep count of who has spent what.

RussianRouletteGuide.strategyIntro: It looks like luck, but how you spend information and credits changes your odds a lot.

strategies.title: Count seats from the muzzle
strategies.body: Number the player the muzzle points at as 1, then 2, 3… clockwise: player k takes chamber k. Match the bullets you know against these numbers to see at once whether you are in danger.

strategies.title: Public inspection is cheap but helps everyone
strategies.body: A 1-credit public inspection gives your rivals the same information. If it shows that you are the one in danger, nobody else has a reason to turn the muzzle for you. For chambers tied to your own seat, paying 2 credits to look privately is safer.

strategies.title: Turning the muzzle shifts every target by one
strategies.body: One turn moves every chamber one player along. If you are in line to be hit, turn to escape; if you are already safe, spending your credits quickly can bring the shots forward before anyone turns it back.

strategies.title: Be the one who fills the pool to 6
strategies.body: Only the player who brings the pool to 6 chooses the swap. Paying 1–2 credits early may just set up someone else's swap. If it looks like others have been paying in, aim to be the one who completes it.

strategies.title: The older the intel, the less you should trust it
strategies.body: A secret swap may have changed chambers you already saw, so at key moments it can be worth checking again. If you made the swap yourself, letting others rely on stale intel is your weapon.

strategies.title: Spending credits decides when the shots come
strategies.body: If you are sure you are safe, spend fast to bring the third player to zero sooner; if you are in danger, save credits to buy time for turns and swaps.

faq.q: Where can I play Russian Roulette?
faq.a: On the PUZZLTHINK Russian Roulette page, right in a desktop or mobile browser, with no sign-up or install.

faq.q: Can I play alone?
faq.a: Yes. The AI game has you and five AI players, and you can choose easy, normal or hard AI.

faq.q: How do I play with friends?
faq.a: Create a friend room and send the link or the 4-digit invite code. AI fills empty seats, and each turn in a friend room lasts 60 seconds.

faq.q: Are the bullet positions really random?
faq.a: Yes. Each game loads two of the six chambers at random and starts the muzzle at a random player. After that, only players' turns and swaps change them.

faq.q: Is it exactly the show's rules?
faq.a: Yes. It uses the same rules as the Russian roulette prison match in The Devil's Plan: Dead Again: six players, six chambers with two bullets, 16 credits, and the same costs for inspecting, turning and swapping, and the same firing order.

RussianJanggiGuide.title: Russian Janggi online — the game from The Society Game 2
RussianJanggiGuide.intro: Russian Janggi is a 3×3 strategy game from the Korean show The Society Game 2. It adds pieces of different sizes to tic-tac-toe: a bigger piece can cover a smaller one like a cup, and pieces on the board can move to another square, so the board can flip until the very last move. The rules are also close to the board game Gobblet Gobblers. Enjoy fast 10-second turns against AI or friends on PUZZLTHINK.
rules: Two players take turns on a 3×3 board.
Each player starts with two large, two medium and two small pieces in hand.
On your turn, either place a piece from your hand, or move one of your pieces that is showing on top to another square.
A piece can go on an empty square or over any smaller piece, yours or your opponent's. Pieces of the same size cannot cover each other.
Three of your pieces showing on top in a row, column or diagonal wins. Covered pieces do not count.
Moving a piece reveals whatever was under it. If that reveals your opponent's line, they win — even if you complete a line of your own at the same moment.
Each turn lasts 10 seconds (the AI game can turn the timer off). If you run out of time or cannot move, the turn passes; after 80 moves the game is a draw.
RussianJanggiGuide.specialTitle: Moments that are easy to misread

special.title: A covered piece has not gone anywhere
special.body: A covered piece is hidden but still on the board. When the piece above it leaves, it shows again and can form a line again. Remembering whose piece sits under each square is half the skill.

special.title: Moving can open your opponent's line
special.body: If your large piece is sitting on an opponent's small piece to block their line, moving it brings that line back and you lose on the spot. Always check what is underneath before you lift a piece.

special.title: A large piece is an unbreakable lid
special.body: Nothing can cover a large piece. Once placed, it holds that square until its owner moves it.

special.title: Pieces left in hand are information too
special.body: If your opponent still holds a large piece, your medium piece can be covered. Keep an eye on both players' hands on screen.

RussianJanggiGuide.strategyTitle: Strategy — a small board with deep play
RussianJanggiGuide.strategyIntro: There are only nine squares, but covering and moving create plenty of options. Here are common ideas.

strategies.title: The center and the value of large pieces
strategies.body: The center square sits on four lines (row, column and both diagonals). Opening with a large piece in the center claims a spot nobody can cover. In simulated AI games the first player won about 58% to 42%.

strategies.title: Keep a large piece for the finish
strategies.body: If you spend both large pieces early, you have nothing to cover back when your opponent covers your small piece with a medium one. Keep one large piece to block a line or to cover your way to a win.

strategies.title: Threaten two lines at once
strategies.body: If one move gives you two pieces on two different lines, your opponent can block only one. Holding a corner and the center makes these forks easier.

strategies.title: Remember who covered whom
strategies.body: Knowing what is covered tells you which pieces your opponent cannot safely move. Their own piece that is blocking their line becomes a chain they cannot lift.

strategies.title: Cover rather than block
strategies.body: When your opponent nearly has a line, covering one of its pieces with a bigger piece is often stronger than filling the empty square, because you break their line and build your own at once.

strategies.title: What to check in 10 seconds
strategies.body: 1) Can your opponent win next move? 2) Can you win now? 3) What is under the piece you want to move? Checking just these three cuts most mistakes.

faq.q: Where can I play Russian Janggi?
faq.a: On the PUZZLTHINK Russian Janggi page, right in a desktop or mobile browser, with no sign-up or install.

faq.q: Where does Russian Janggi come from?
faq.a: It appeared on tvN's The Society Game 2. PUZZLTHINK is an unofficial fan project that introduces the game and lets you play it on the web.

faq.q: Is it like Gobblet Gobblers?
faq.a: It is in a similar family: pieces of different sizes cover and move to make three in a row. PUZZLTHINK's Russian Janggi follows the format from The Society Game 2, with two pieces of each size per player and a 10-second turn.

faq.q: Can it end in a draw?
faq.a: Pieces can keep moving back and forth, so the game is a draw after 80 moves. It is also a draw when neither player can move.

faq.q: Does going first help?
faq.a: A little, because the first player can take the center. In the AI game you can choose who goes first: you, the AI, or random.

BlindGomokuGuide.title: Blind Gomoku — black and white hidden under colour
BlindGomokuGuide.intro: Blind Gomoku is a gomoku variant inspired by the blind gomoku game from Netflix's The Devil's Plan. Every stone shows one of seven colours on top; black and white are marked only underneath. Your opponent always plays the same colour you just used, so the board alone never tells you whose stone is whose. It comes down to memory and deduction. Play 1:1 against the AI, or 1:1 with a friend by invite link or 4-digit code.
rules: On a 15×15 board, black (first) and white (second) take turns. Against the AI you are black; with a friend, colours are drawn at random.
Each turn black picks red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple or pink.
White plays the same outer colour black just used. The AI follows this rule too.
Only colours show on the board. You see black and white only when you peek: twice a game, 5 seconds each, on your turn.
Free gomoku rules: no forbidden 3-3 or 4-4, and six or more in a row also wins.
Whoever first makes five or more in a row wins; the board flips and the winning line is drawn. A full board is a draw.
Friend games have a turn clock (30, 60 or 90 s): on time out a move is made for you, and three in a row loses on time.

special.title: Same colours come in pairs
special.body: White copies black's colour right away, so stones of one colour usually come as one black and one white. Reusing a colour creates several pairs and gets confusing.

special.title: Your opponent may already have four
special.body: If your memory slips, you may mistake their stone for yours and not block. The moment they make five, the board flips and the game ends.

special.title: Peeks only on your turn
special.body: You can peek only when it's your move, and you can't play while looking. In friend games your clock keeps running while you look.

special.title: The AI's memory
special.body: AI difficulty is memory: easy remembers the last 3 moves, normal the last 8, hard the last 24. Building on old stones can catch the AI out.

BlindGomokuGuide.strategyIntro: In blind gomoku, managing your memory matters as much as gomoku skill. Common tricks:

strategies.title: Give colours a job
strategies.body: For example, 'red and orange attack, blue and purple defend'. Your opponent uses the same colours, but your own scheme helps you recall what you put where.

strategies.title: One line, one colour
strategies.body: Building a line in one colour makes it easy to remember it's yours. White drops the same colour nearby, so if a line mixes in that colour, recall the order of moves.

strategies.title: Mix colours to confuse
strategies.body: In friend games your opponent relies on memory too. As black, switch colours now and then so they lose track of your line, but not so much that you lose track yourself.

strategies.title: Peek in the middle game
strategies.body: Early on, memory is enough. Peek when there are 20 to 30 stones and you think 'is this four in a row?'. Keep the last peek for the decisive moment.

strategies.title: When unsure, block
strategies.body: If you see a line of four and aren't sure whose it is, block it. Blocking your own line costs far less than letting them make five.

strategies.title: Revive old stones
strategies.body: The AI forgets old moves (even hard keeps only the last 24). Finishing a line that connects to your early stones often goes unblocked.

strategies.title: Flip the board to review
strategies.body: After the game, flip freely between the colour side and the black-and-white side while stepping through moves. The colour side shows what you saw; the other shows what was really there.

NemoCountGuide.title: Nemo Count — the Devil's Plan counting game, and how to count fast
NemoCountGuide.intro: Nemo Count is the counting game from Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again (season 3). On a board of cells, count how many rectangles have numbers adding up to the target. The rule is simple, but missing one or counting one twice is a wrong answer, so a systematic way of counting decides it. PUZZLTHINK generates boards at random and computes every answer and solution, so there is always a new board.
rules: The board is made of square cells; some carry numbers. Blank cells are 0.
A nemo is a rectangle of whole cells. Squares and single cells count; it may not leave the board or cross a gap.
A rectangle counts once if its numbers add up exactly to the target.
Solo: the 30-minute challenge allows one answer per board, and a pass moves straight on; your number of correct answers is recorded. Practice has no time limit.

Friends (2–6): the first to buzz answers within 10 seconds. A wrong answer does not knock you out; buzz again after 3 seconds. A pass proposes skipping the board and goes through only if everyone else agrees (one agreed pass per player per game).

A friend game moves on when someone is right, a pass is agreed, or the time per board (1–5 min or none) runs out. After the set number of boards, most correct answers wins, then the shorter total time.

special.title: A single cell is a nemo
special.body: A cell whose number equals the target is one rectangle. With target 0, every blank cell counts.

special.title: Not only squares
special.body: Rectangles like 1×3 or 2×4 count too. Counting by size keeps you from missing any.

special.title: No crossing gaps
special.body: Boards have uneven shapes, so every cell of a rectangle must be on the board.

special.title: Numbers above the target are walls
special.body: No number is negative, so a cell bigger than the target can never be inside a counted rectangle. Split the board around it.

NemoCountGuide.strategyIntro: On the show, the order of counting mattered more than arithmetic. Common methods:

strategies.title: Full blocks by formula
strategies.body: A blank block a cells wide and b tall holds a(a+1)/2 × b(b+1)/2 rectangles; a 3×3 holds 6×6 = 36. For target 0, split into blocks, use the formula, and add the rectangles that span blocks.

strategies.title: Anchor on the top-left cell
strategies.body: Every rectangle has exactly one top-left cell. Count, cell by cell, only the rectangles starting there and you will never count one twice.

strategies.title: Singles, rows, columns, then blocks
strategies.body: Count single cells first, then 1×2 and 1×3 rows, then columns, then 2×2 and up. The solution replay walks in the same order, smallest first.

strategies.title: Stop when the sum overflows
strategies.body: There are no negatives, so once a growing rectangle passes the target, that direction is done. Big numbers cut things short quickly.

strategies.title: Split the board at the 1s
strategies.body: With target 0, every numbered cell is a wall. Cut the board into pieces at those cells, count each piece by formula, then the rectangles that cross between pieces.

strategies.title: Review misses with the replay
strategies.body: In practice, Show answer outlines each rectangle in turn. Seeing which size you missed lifts your accuracy fast.

BlackWhiteGuide.title: Black & White — hide the numbers, read the colours
BlackWhiteGuide.intro: Black & White is a two-player mind game from a death match in The Genius: Rule Breaker. Both players hold the same tiles 0 to 8 and lay one at a time; the higher number wins. But your rival's numbers are never shown, only black or white, so the game becomes a battle over when to spend a big tile and when to throw one away. On PUZZLTHINK you can play a three-level AI or a friend 1:1 by link or 4-digit code, and turn every tile over at the end to replay the game round by round.
rules: Each player gets nine tiles, 0 to 8. Even tiles (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) are black; odd tiles (1, 3, 5, 7) are white.
The round-1 leader is chosen at random. The leader lays a tile face down and only its colour is shown.
The other player sees that colour and lays a tile of their own.
The higher number scores one point. Equal numbers are a draw and nobody scores.
Only the result (win, loss or draw) is announced; the numbers stay hidden until the end.
The round winner leads the next round. After a draw the same player leads again.
The game ends after nine rounds, or once the lead is bigger than the rounds left. Equal scores are a draw.
Friend games have a turn timer (15, 30 or 60 s); when it runs out a random tile is played, and three in a row lose.

special.body: Black has five tiles (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) and white four (1, 3, 5, 7). Both the strongest 8 and the weakest 0 are black, so a black tile might be either.

special.title: 0 always loses, but…
special.body: 0 beats nothing and only draws with another 0. Yet if it makes your rival spend an 8, one cheap tile has wiped out their strongest.

special.title: Equal numbers draw
special.body: If both play the same number it's a draw and the leader stays. Equal numbers share a colour, so it can only happen when you answer in the same colour.

special.title: It can end early
special.body: Leading 5–2 with two rounds left can't be caught, so the game ends at once. Tiles never played are shown in the replay too.

BlackWhiteGuide.strategyIntro: It looks like luck, but tracking the tiles left and reading habits clearly raises your win rate.

strategies.title: Count their colours first
strategies.body: How many black and white tiles your rival has used stays on screen. If they have one black left and lay black, you may know the exact number. Cross numbers out in the notes.

strategies.title: Narrow it down with results
strategies.body: If their black lost to your 5 it was 0, 2 or 4; if it won, 6 or 8. Every result shrinks the range.

BlackWhite2Guide.title: Black & White II — read the numbers between the gauge lights
BlackWhite2Guide.intro: A two-player blind-bidding game about dividing 99 points across nine rounds. You see only your rival's black-or-white bid and their remaining-point band, so the central skill is winning narrowly while making them lose expensively. Play three AI levels or invite a friend by link or 4-digit code, then review every bid and mind game at the end.
rules: Both players receive 99 points for up to nine rounds. Each round you may bid anything from zero to everything left; spent points are gone.
After the round-one leader is chosen, they bid first. A bid from 0 to 9 appears black and a bid of 10 or more appears white.
The leader's points are deducted and their five-step gauge updates immediately. The other player sees the colour and new gauge before replying.
The higher bid scores one and leads next. Equal bids score nothing and the existing leader stays.
The five gauge bands are 0–19, 20–39, 40–59, 60–79 and 80–99. Only you know your exact total.
The first player to five wins immediately; otherwise the higher score after round nine wins.
If round nine ends level, old points vanish and both players receive 33 fresh points for a best-of-three overtime.
Friend rooms use a turn timer; three consecutive timeouts lose the game.

special.title: Zero is a legal bid
special.body: Zero appears black and costs nothing. It rarely wins, but can bait a white or otherwise large reply for free.

special.title: The gauge changes after the lead bid
special.body: If the leader falls from 79 to 59, the replying player sees two lights disappear before choosing. That instant information is central to the game.

special.title: A tie keeps the leader
special.body: Equal bids score nothing and the same player leads again next round. Both bids are still spent.

special.title: Overtime starts from a fresh 33
special.body: Nothing carries over from the main game. Both totals reset to 33 for a best-of-three overtime.

BlackWhite2Guide.strategyTitle: Tips — win cheaply, make losses expensive
BlackWhite2Guide.strategyIntro: There is no fixed arithmetic solution. The game is about moving your rival's threshold with limited public information.

strategies.title: Win by one when you can
strategies.body: Beating 10 with 11 gives the same point as beating it with 40. Once you know the likely range, use the smallest winning bid.

strategies.title: Lose cheaply in black
strategies.body: A 0–9 bid that draws out 10 or more gives up one round but creates a bank advantage you can turn into gauge pressure later.

strategies.title: Black does not always demand 10
strategies.body: Ten guarantees a win over black, but only beats 9 by one. Decide whether to chase a tie with 9 or buy certainty with 10.

strategies.title: Bluff around gauge boundaries
strategies.body: Exact totals remain hidden inside each band. Stay just above a boundary or knock off several lights at once to disrupt your rival's estimate.

strategies.title: Black gets dangerous against four points
strategies.body: At 2–4 or 3–4, a leading black can be stopped by a reply of 10. Budget roughly ten defensive points for each point you trail.

strategies.title: At 4–4, the larger bank has power
strategies.body: On the last round, the player with more left can always bid higher. Plan not only for early points, but for your final spendable total.

PiggyBankGuide.title: Piggy Bank — remember and doubt
PiggyBankGuide.intro: Piggy Bank is a four-player memory game based on a prison match from Netflix's The Devil's Plan: Dead Again. Every coin drop is announced truthfully but never written down, so you must remember who put what into which bank. On PUZZLTHINK you play against three AI players with different memories.
rules: Banks start with 1 black and 1 white coin. Banks 1–4 go into each player's lower slot, bank 5 onto the first player's top slot.
On your turn put 1–5 coins into your lower bank and announce exactly what you put in.
Hand that bank to anyone: it goes to their top slot, and your top bank drops into your lower slot.
The receiver says how many coins of the asked colour their top bank holds, within 20 seconds. The colour alternates black → white → black.
Everyone else picks Doubt or No doubt within 10 seconds. If all pass, play moves on and the receiver takes the next turn.
A doubted bank is opened: if the answer was wrong the doubter gets +1 and the answerer −1; if it was right the doubter loses 1.
The opened bank leaves the game; whoever lost a point gets a new bank (1 black, 1 white, next number) on top and takes the turn.
When three players press reset, every bank goes back to 1 black and 1 white; anyone who didn't press may first try to name every bank (+3 / −2).
The game ends when someone reaches 5 points; players are ranked by score.

special.title: Shown briefly, never logged
special.body: Coin drops appear for a few seconds and then vanish. There's no log or notepad — it's all memory.

special.body: No answer within 20 seconds counts as 0. Others can still doubt it.

special.title: Reset keeps the score

PiggyBankGuide.strategyTitle: Tips — shake their memory, doubt only when sure
PiggyBankGuide.strategyIntro: Piggy Bank is as much about protecting your memory as disturbing everyone else's.

strategies.title: One line per bank
strategies.body: Pair each number with its counts, like "5: 3 black 2 white", and update that line every drop.

strategies.title: Pass the busy banks
strategies.body: Banks that took many drops are the easiest to get wrong. Hand them to whoever seems least sure.

strategies.title: Only when certain
strategies.body: A wrong doubt costs you a point. Doubt only on banks you're sure of.

strategies.title: Read the reset
strategies.body: Resets come when memories blur. If you know every bank, don't press — go for the +3 all-in guess.

HexagonGuide.title: Hexagon — The Devil's Plan final, and how to hold 19 numbers
HexagonGuide.intro: Hexagon was the second game of the final of Netflix's The Devil's Plan season 1. You memorize the numbers on 19 hexagons for 30 seconds; then the board flips to its letters and you name the straight lines of three whose numbers add up to the target. On the show no round was ever fully solved. On PUZZLTHINK you can play random boards or the ten boards from the broadcast.
rules: The board is 19 hexagons in rows of 3, 4, 5, 4 and 3. Fronts show numbers, backs show the letters A to S.
Each round the fronts are shown for 30 seconds, then the board flips and the target number appears.
Three neighbouring tiles in a straight line, across or along either diagonal, whose numbers add up to the target are an answer. A board has 27 such lines.
Right is +1, wrong is −1. Repeating an answer already given, or (with friends) not declaring within 10 seconds of buzzing, is wrong too.
Declared answers are not marked on the board, and the number of answers is not revealed.
A round ends when every answer is out or after 90 seconds without a declaration, then the answers are shown. Solo is 10 rounds; the challenge runs for 10 minutes.

special.title: No bends
special.body: The three tiles must run straight in one direction. Three touching tiles that bend at the middle are not a line.

special.title: Order does not matter
special.body: Q-R-S and S-R-Q are the same answer; tiles are judged whatever order you tap them in.

special.title: Remember what was given
special.body: Nothing stays marked, so repeating an earlier answer costs a point. Memorize the declared answers as well as the numbers.

special.title: There are only a few answers
special.body: On the show each round had 1–6 answers; random boards here have 2–5. If you are not sure, staying quiet is a strategy.

HexagonGuide.strategyTitle: Tips — how you memorize decides it
HexagonGuide.strategyIntro: In the final, memory and composure mattered more than arithmetic. Common approaches:

strategies.title: Chunk the rows
strategies.body: Remember rows as chunks like '163' and '2456', the way you would a phone number. 19 tiles fit in 30 seconds more easily.

strategies.title: Pre-add some lines
strategies.body: You cannot add all 27 lines, but knowing the sums of the 9 across-lines lets you call some answers as soon as the target shows.

strategies.title: The centre tile J is in 6 lines
strategies.body: The middle tile is used by the most lines. Make sure of the central numbers before the edges.

strategies.title: A wrong answer erases a right one
strategies.body: With +1 and −1, a half-sure guess loses on average. The show's analysis that avoiding wrong calls matters most was right.

strategies.title: Easy ones first
strategies.body: With friends, whoever buzzes first takes the answer. Found one sure line? Buzz right away.

strategies.title: Warm up on the broadcast boards

SlitherlinkGuide.intro: Slitherlink is a logic puzzle played on a grid of dots: draw a single unbroken loop. A number in a cell says how many of its four sides the loop runs along. PUZZLTHINK makes a fresh board with exactly one answer every time.

All lines must join into one closed loop: no branches (three lines at a dot) and no loose ends.
A numbered cell has exactly that many of its sides on the loop.
Cells without a number have no limit.
Practice offers 9×9, 10×10 and 11×11 (show size) dot boards, with unlimited hints.

WallGo2Guide.title: Wallgo II — splitting the board with square and round pieces
WallGo2Guide.intro: Wallgo II from The Devil's Plan 3 prison match, episode 10. As in Wallgo you move pieces and build walls to claim the largest territory, but there are now two kinds of piece and no staying put, so every move counts. Play 3-player or 1:1 vs AI, invite friends with a link or 4-digit code, or open a public room, and replay the game afterwards.
rules: Build walls on a 7×7 board to make your territory the largest.
Round 1 is a 3-player game. Each player gets one square and one round piece. In turn order each player places one of them on an empty tile; the second pieces go down in reverse order.
A square piece moves 1–2 tiles in one direction. A round piece moves 1 tile and may then turn left or right for 1 more tile.
On your turn you have 90 seconds to move a piece and then build a wall. You cannot move onto another piece or through a wall.
In round 1 only, each player may once knock down a wall on the path and move through it.
After moving, build a wall on one side of that piece. A side that already has a wall cannot take another; if time runs out a wall goes on a random side.
The game ends the moment every player's pieces are walled apart, even if someone never used their wall break.
Add up the tiles of the areas your pieces are in; the most wins. On a tie, the bigger single area ranks higher.
Round 2 is 1:1. The player with more territory in round 1 goes first. Each starts with 2 square and 2 round pieces, the round ones on fixed tiles. There is no wall break.

special.title: No staying put
special.body: Unlike Wallgo, you must move. A piece with nowhere to go cannot be picked, and if neither of your pieces can move, your turn is skipped.

special.title: Round pieces cannot go 2 straight
special.body: A round piece moves 1 tile and may only turn, so it ends up 1 tile away or diagonally. Two straight tiles is a square-piece move.

special.title: Wall break is on the path
special.body: You may break any one wall on the path you take, not just one next to the piece. Tiles you can only reach by breaking are shown in red.

special.title: Ties go to the big room
special.body: If two players have the same total, the size of their largest single area decides. One big room beats several small ones.

WallGo2Guide.strategyTitle: Tips — play to each piece's strength
WallGo2Guide.strategyIntro: Square pieces reach far to cut off a lane; round pieces turn corners to slip out of tight spots.

strategies.title: Round piece near the centre
strategies.body: Round pieces can turn, so they are hard to trap. Near the centre they can break out in any direction.

strategies.title: Cut lanes with the square
strategies.body: A square piece can travel two tiles straight and wall off a lane in one turn.

strategies.title: Save the break for an escape
strategies.body: You get one break. It is worth most when your piece is about to be shut in a small room and can punch through to a bigger one.

strategies.title: Guard one big room
strategies.body: Ties are settled by the largest area, so keeping one big room is safer than splitting into many.

faq.q: How is it different from Wallgo?
faq.a: There are square and round pieces that move differently, no staying put, the wall break works on the path, and ties are settled by the largest area.

faq.q: Can I play alone?
faq.a: Yes. Play 3-player against 2 AI or 1:1 against 1 AI, on easy, normal or hard.

faq.q: How do I play with friends?
faq.a: Create a room under Play with friends and send the link or 4-digit code. You can also open a public room in Open match.

faq.q: Where do the round pieces start in round 2?
faq.a: Each player's two round pieces start on fixed tiles facing each other diagonally; you only place the two square pieces.

MorrisGuide.title: Nine Men's Morris — mill, take, fly
MorrisGuide.intro: Nine Men's Morris is a board game from Roman times that drew new fans as the first game of the final in Netflix's The Devil's Plan season 1. Each player places and moves nine pieces on 24 points joined by three nested squares, taking an enemy piece with every line of three. The rules are short, but the fight for points while placing and the reading while moving run deep. Play it on PUZZLTHINK against the AI or with a friend by invite link or 4-digit code, best of three.
rules: The board has 24 points joined by lines. Black and white have nine pieces each; black goes first.
Placing: take turns putting one piece on an empty point. Pieces cannot move until all nine are placed.
Moving: after that, each turn move one piece one step along a line to a free neighbouring point.
Mills: three of yours on a straight line take one enemy piece. Pieces in your opponent's mills cannot be taken.
Flying: once placing is over and you are down to three pieces, you may move to any empty point.
Losing: two pieces left, or no piece that can move on your turn, loses the round.
Deadlock: once someone has three pieces, ten turns without a capture end the round; fewer pieces loses, equal is a draw.
Best of three, colours swap every round. Friend games have a 30/60/90s turn clock with an automatic move on time out.

special.title: Two mills at once
special.body: Even when one move closes two mills, you take only one piece.

special.title: Every enemy piece in a mill
special.body: As on the show, pieces in a mill are safe — if all of them are, this mill takes nothing.

special.title: Boxed in after placing
special.body: You can't get stuck while placing, but if all your pieces are blocked once placing ends, you lose on your first moving turn.

special.title: Flying needs exactly three
special.body: You fly only after placing, with exactly three pieces on the board. A flying opponent can block your mill point from anywhere.

MorrisGuide.strategyIntro: Games are won by taking good points while placing and by running mills while moving.

strategies.title: Take the junctions
strategies.body: Points with four neighbours (D6, B4, F4, D2) are the most flexible once moving starts. Take them before rushing a mill.

strategies.title: Don't get boxed in
strategies.body: If nothing can move when placing ends, you lose. Don't crowd your pieces into corners surrounded by enemy pieces.

strategies.title: Run a mill
strategies.body: Step one piece out of a mill and back in on your next turn to take a piece every time — as long as your opponent cannot fill the gap.

strategies.title: Double mill
strategies.body: Set up a piece that closes one mill or the other every time it moves, and there is no defence.

strategies.title: Block two-in-a-row
strategies.body: Two enemy pieces on a line with the third point free is a mill next turn. Block it, especially while placing.

strategies.title: Fly to block
strategies.body: With three pieces you can block a mill point anywhere. But with the ten-turn deadlock rule, time isn't on your side if you have fewer pieces.

faq.q: Where can I play Nine Men's Morris?
faq.a: On PUZZLTHINK's Nine Men's Morris page, in any PC or mobile browser, with no sign-up or install.

faq.q: How do I play with a friend?
faq.a: Create a room with 'Play with a friend' to get an invite link and a 4-digit code. Your friend opens the link or enters the code.

faq.q: Are these the Devil's Plan rules?
faq.a: Yes: nine pieces, pieces in mills are safe, fly with three, lose with two, a 10-turn deadlock with three left goes to the side with more pieces, best of three. Instead of piece benefits, colours swap each round.

faq.q: How strong is the AI?
faq.a: Easy slips now and then, normal looks three moves ahead, hard five or more. Beat hard to earn a hard-clear certificate.

rules: Players take turns placing one stone on a 15×15 board, red first.
Close 1–2 enemy stones in a straight line between two of yours and they flip to your colour (8 directions). A run of 3 or more is too heavy to flip.
The stone your opponent just placed (gold ring) can't be flipped on your very next move, so a block always holds for a turn.
Flipped stones keep the other colour as their eyes. Five of your colour in a row wins — but a five may hold at most one flipped stone.
